items.prompt: Priya and Marco argue about the job queue for three days in a Slack thread with 40+ replies and no decision. What is the thread genuinely good at, and what is it bad at?
choices: Good at nothing at all; per this reasoning the thread format itself is always the actual problem
Good at surfacing objections quickly; bad at closing, because nothing in the format forces a decision
Good at reaching a decision quickly; bad at actually letting people raise real objections
Good and bad at exactly the same specific things an RFC document would be
items.explanation: A live thread lowers the friction to raise a point, which is genuinely useful. What it lacks is any built-in mechanism for ending — no shared document, no stated decision owner, no moment where silence means agreement instead of 'I haven't read it yet.' That gap, not the arguing itself, is what an RFC process is built to close.
items.reference:
Live thread

Fast to start, never closes

RFC

Slower to start, forces a decision

Why: arguing well and deciding well are different skills — a format can be good at one and bad at the other.

items.prompt: A teammate says 'we don't need RFCs, we just need to argue less.' What's the flaw in that framing, based on what actually went wrong in Priya and Marco's thread?
choices: Nothing is wrong with that framing — arguing less would have fixed the underlying problem just as well
The problem wasn't the amount of arguing, it was that nothing in the format ever closed the argument into a decision
RFCs, according to this framing, exist specifically and only to reduce how much people disagree
The thread would most likely have worked out fine with simply a stricter reply limit in place
items.explanation: Fewer messages wouldn't have produced a decision on their own — the thread could have gone quiet after 5 messages instead of 40 and still left nobody sure what was decided. The fix isn't less disagreement, it's a format that turns disagreement into a recorded decision.
items.reference:
Live thread

Fast to start, never closes

RFC

Slower to start, forces a decision

Why: arguing well and deciding well are different skills — a format can be good at one and bad at the other.

items.prompt: What is the main cost an RFC pays that a live thread doesn't?
choices: It takes real time to write upfront, before any discussion even starts
It prevents anyone from raising objections
It requires management approval before anyone can comment
It cannot be used for reversible, low-stakes decisions
items.explanation: Writing a real RFC — context, options, trade-offs — takes actual upfront time that a two-line Slack message doesn't. That's exactly why RFCs are worth reserving for expensive-to-reverse decisions rather than every choice a team makes; the L1 table's 'bad at speed' row is the honest cost side of the trade.
items.reference:
Live thread

Fast to start, never closes

RFC

Slower to start, forces a decision

Why: arguing well and deciding well are different skills — a format can be good at one and bad at the other.

items.prompt: What does an RFC / design doc add that a live conversation about the same proposal doesn't have?
choices: A single written place holding the proposal, alternatives, and trade-offs, that people comment on asynchronously and that ends in a recorded decision
A guarantee, built into the format itself, that everyone involved will ultimately agree with whatever is proposed
A faster way of reaching essentially the same conclusion that a live chat thread would eventually have reached anyway
A structured way to avoid ever having to write down any disagreement that comes up during the review
items.explanation: An RFC is a document, not a debate format — its value is holding the full picture in one place and ending with an explicit decision written into the document, which a scattered thread of replies structurally can't do.
items.reference:
An RFC holds:

  • The proposal
  • Alternatives considered
  • Trade-offs
  • The final decision

Why: a document that ends in a decision is what a thread of replies structurally cannot produce on its own.

items.prompt: A teammate writes a one-paragraph proposal with no alternatives listed and no trade-offs section, and calls it an RFC. What's missing?
choices: Nothing is really missing — length alone isn't what makes something qualify as an RFC
The parts that let a reviewer actually evaluate the reasoning: what else was considered, and what each option costs
A list naming everyone who has to formally approve it before anyone else is allowed to comment
A guarantee, stated somewhere in the doc, that it will be accepted without any objections at all
items.explanation: Calling something an RFC doesn't make it one if it skips the parts that let a reviewer form an independent opinion — alternatives considered and their trade-offs. A one-paragraph pitch with only the author's conclusion is closer to an announcement than a request for comments.
items.reference:
An RFC holds:

  • The proposal
  • Alternatives considered
  • Trade-offs
  • The final decision

Why: a document that ends in a decision is what a thread of replies structurally cannot produce on its own.

items.prompt: Why does an RFC end with a decision written into the document itself, rather than just leaving the last comment as the de facto answer?
choices: So there's a single, unambiguous place to point to later when someone asks 'what did we actually agree to?'
Because comments are automatically deleted after a week
It doesn't matter where the decision lives, as long as someone remembers it
So the author can avoid ever being asked to justify the choice
items.explanation: A decision buried in the middle of a long comment thread is exactly as hard to find later as a decision buried in 40 Slack replies. Writing it into the document itself — usually a short 'Status: Accepted' line plus reasoning — is what makes the decision retrievable months later.
items.reference:
An RFC holds:

  • The proposal
  • Alternatives considered
  • Trade-offs
  • The final decision

Why: a document that ends in a decision is what a thread of replies structurally cannot produce on its own.

items.prompt: What does 'disagree-and-commit' actually ask of someone whose position lost?
choices: State the objection once for the record, then execute the decided direction at full effort instead of relitigating it
Publicly agree out loud that they were wrong, even if they privately still think they were right
Simply stop working on the project altogether once their position has lost
Keep raising that exact same objection repeatedly until the decision eventually gets reversed
items.explanation: Disagree-and-commit doesn't require pretending to agree — it requires putting the objection on record once, then building the decided thing without a slower, resentful implementation or repeated relitigating. The objection stays visible in the record; it just stops being an active blocker.
items.reference:
Commit means

State it once → build it fully

Commit does NOT mean

Pretend to agree, or quietly under-build it

items.prompt: Marco lost the SQS vs. Redis decision but keeps building the SQS integration noticeably slower and less carefully than his other work. Is this consistent with disagree-and-commit?
choices: Yes — commit only requires not blocking the decision, effort level is a separate matter
No — commit means building the decided direction at full effort, not a quiet, under-resourced version of it
Yes, as long as he doesn't say anything negative about the decision out loud
It depends on whether Marco's objection was ever answered
items.explanation: Slow-walking or under-investing in a decision you disagreed with is a real, if quiet, way of not committing — it's just relitigating by other means. Genuine commit means the same care and effort as if the decision had been Marco's own idea.
items.reference:
Commit means

State it once → build it fully

Commit does NOT mean

Pretend to agree, or quietly under-build it

items.prompt: Why does disagree-and-commit require the objection to be stated on the record before someone commits, rather than just asking everyone to move on quietly?
choices: So the objection is visible to whoever reviews the decision later, instead of disappearing entirely
It genuinely doesn't matter — staying silent and stating an objection lead to the exact same outcome
So that the objection can later be used to overturn the decision at any point without needing new evidence
Because leaving an objection unstated is, per this unit, illegal in most engineering organizations
items.explanation: A stated objection becomes part of the decision's record — useful if the concern turns out to matter later, and proof the decision was made with eyes open. A quietly dropped objection just vanishes, which is the 'silent disagreement' anti-pattern from L3, not commit.
items.reference:
Commit means

State it once → build it fully

Commit does NOT mean

Pretend to agree, or quietly under-build it

items.prompt: Two engineers disagree on whether a linter rule should be 'warn' or 'error.' Does this need an RFC?
choices: Yes, per this reasoning every single technical disagreement needs a fully written RFC
Probably not — it's a small, cheap-to-reverse choice, and writing a document would cost more than the decision is worth
Only if a manager happens to specifically request that one be written for this case
Only if the disagreement happens to drag on for more than a single day
items.explanation: RFCs earn their upfront writing cost on expensive-to-reverse decisions — a data store, a public API shape, a service boundary. A linter setting is cheap to flip back if it's wrong, so the overhead of a full document isn't worth paying.
items.reference:
Write an RFC when: expensive to reverse (data store, public API, service boundary).
Skip it when: small and cheap to undo (naming, a lint rule).

items.prompt: What kind of decision is most worth the upfront cost of writing a full RFC?
choices: One that's expensive or slow to reverse once built, like a data store migration or a public API shape
Any decision at all, genuinely regardless of how easy or cheap it would be to undo later
Only decisions where a manager happens to be personally and directly involved
Decisions that, as it happens, nobody on the team actually has a strong opinion about
items.explanation: The RFC's overhead pays for itself specifically when getting the decision wrong would be costly to walk back later. Cheap, reversible choices don't need that insurance — the cost of writing the document would exceed the cost of just trying it and adjusting.
items.reference:
Write an RFC when: expensive to reverse (data store, public API, service boundary).
Skip it when: small and cheap to undo (naming, a lint rule).

items.prompt: Why does L1 argue that closing a disagreement matters as much as raising it in the first place?
choices: Because a team that argues well but never decides still pays the full cost of the argument without getting the one thing it was for — an actual direction to build in
Because closing a disagreement quickly is treated here as, in every single case, always more important than actually getting it right
Because raising objections is treated as easy here, while actually closing them out is described as essentially impossible
Because closing is said here to not actually matter at all in this model — only the initial act of raising the objection does
items.explanation: Time, tension, and attention spent arguing are real costs whether or not the argument ends in a decision. A process that's great at surfacing disagreement but never resolves it pays those costs for nothing — closing is what converts the cost of arguing into the benefit of a direction.
items.reference: Arguing without closing = full cost of the argument, none of the benefit of a decision.

items.prompt: A team prides itself on 'we always hear everyone out' but three of their last five technical debates ended with no recorded decision. What's the actual gap in their process?
choices: They're good at raising objections but missing the mechanism that turns discussion into a decision
They hear out far too many people and should instead limit who's allowed to comment on a proposal
There genuinely is no gap here — hearing everyone out is treated as the entire point of the process
The real problem, per this framing, is that they simply don't argue enough before actually deciding
items.explanation: Hearing everyone out is the input half of the process working correctly. The missing half is closing — a named decision owner and an explicit moment where the discussion converts into a written decision, which is exactly what an RFC's lifecycle stages are built to force.
items.reference: Arguing without closing = full cost of the argument, none of the benefit of a decision.

items.prompt: What's the exit condition for the 'Request comments' stage of the RFC lifecycle?
choices: The review window closes, or every open thread has been addressed
At least ten distinct people have left some form of comment on the document
The author of the RFC personally feels fully satisfied with how the document reads
There is, per the lifecycle as described, no real exit condition — this stage never formally ends
items.explanation: Request comments ends when the stated review window closes (or every open thread is resolved) — an explicit, checkable condition, not a vague sense that 'enough people have looked at it,' which is what keeps the stage from dragging on indefinitely.
items.reference:
DraftAuthor ready for wider eyes
Request commentsWindow closes / threads addressed
DiscussionNo new blocking objections
DecisionWritten into the doc
CommitWork starts

items.prompt: What actually marks the transition from 'Discussion' to 'Decision' in the lifecycle?
choices: No new blocking objections are being raised, so the owner can pick an option
Exactly 5 business days have passed on the calendar, regardless of any open objections remaining
Every single commenter on the thread has explicitly typed out the words 'I agree'
The author simply decides, on their own judgment, that discussion is over whenever they feel like it
items.explanation: Discussion's exit condition is the absence of new blocking objections, not a fixed clock or unanimous agreement (which may never arrive). Non-blocking comments and disagreement in principle don't hold up this transition — only unresolved, concrete objections do.
items.reference:
DraftAuthor ready for wider eyes
Request commentsWindow closes / threads addressed
DiscussionNo new blocking objections
DecisionWritten into the doc
CommitWork starts

items.prompt: An RFC has zero remaining objections and the review window has closed, but no 'Decision' section has been written. According to the lifecycle, has this RFC reached the commit stage?
choices: No — the decision stage requires the outcome to actually be written into the document; silence alone isn't a decision
Yes — silence after the window closes automatically means acceptance
Yes, as long as the author privately believes it's approved
It depends on how many people originally commented
items.explanation: Every stage in the lifecycle has an explicit exit condition, and Decision's is a written outcome — not just quiet. Without that, the team is back to the live-thread failure mode of an unrecorded, hard-to-point-to 'agreement.'
items.reference:
DraftAuthor ready for wider eyes
Request commentsWindow closes / threads addressed
DiscussionNo new blocking objections
DecisionWritten into the doc
CommitWork starts

items.prompt: Why does the review window need a stated length (e.g. '5 business days') instead of just staying open until people stop commenting?
choices: An open-ended window never gives silence a meaning — a fixed window lets the team treat unbroken silence by the deadline as no-objection
A stated length is, per this reasoning, only ever useful for internal legal record-keeping purposes
It genuinely doesn't matter, since most real objections tend to arrive within the very first hour anyway
Fixed review windows are, according to this unit, a technical requirement of version control systems
items.explanation: Without a stated deadline, silence is ambiguous — it could mean agreement or it could mean nobody's read it yet. A fixed window converts silence-by-the-deadline into an actual, usable signal, which is what lets the Discussion stage actually close.
items.reference:
No deadline: silence is ambiguous.
Fixed window: silence by the deadline = no objection.

items.prompt: A team leaves every RFC's review window open indefinitely, arguing this gives everyone maximum chance to comment. What's the hidden cost of this choice?
choices: It reproduces the live-thread failure mode from L1 — there's no moment where silence reliably means agreement, so the document can drift without ever formally closing
There is, in fact, no real cost here at all according to this framing — giving people more time to comment is strictly and always better
It makes objections raised at any point during that open window measurably more likely to end up being counted as blocking
It conveniently removes, according to this reasoning, the need for the RFC to ever have a single, clearly named decision owner
items.explanation: Maximum comment opportunity sounds generous, but without a deadline the document never gets a clean signal that review is done — it just quietly stops getting attention, which is functionally the same failure L1's 40-message thread had, just spread over a document instead of a chat window.
items.reference:
No deadline: silence is ambiguous.
Fixed window: silence by the deadline = no objection.

items.prompt: Why does an RFC need an 'Options considered' section even when the author already knows which option they want?
choices: It lets a reviewer evaluate the reasoning, not just the conclusion — and it's often exactly where a real objection gets caught
It's really just a formality with no genuine effect on the actual quality of the review that follows
It's only ever needed in cases where the author themselves is unsure which option to ultimately pick
It exists mainly to make the finished document look longer and superficially more thorough
items.explanation: A document with only one option isn't really requesting review — it's asking for approval of a decision already made. Showing the rejected alternatives, and why they lost, is what gives a reviewer the material to independently judge the reasoning, sometimes catching an error the author missed.
items.reference:
• Context / problem
  • Options considered
  • Trade-offs (every option, including the pick)
  • Recommendation
  • Non-goals
  • Decision (added later)

items.prompt: An RFC's trade-off table lists costs and risks for the two rejected options, but leaves the recommended option's row blank. What's wrong with this?
choices: It only scrutinizes the options being rejected, so a reader can't trust the comparison — the recommended option needs the same honest accounting
Nothing is actually wrong here — the recommended option doesn't need its trade-offs listed since it already won
It's perfectly fine as long as the recommendation itself is stated clearly enough somewhere else in the doc
This is, in fact, the standard and fully expected format that any trade-off table should follow
items.explanation: Rating every option the same way, including the author's own pick, is what makes a trade-off table honest rather than a sales pitch. Leaving the favored option's costs out hides exactly the information a skeptical reviewer needs to evaluate the recommendation fairly.
items.reference:
• Context / problem
  • Options considered
  • Trade-offs (every option, including the pick)
  • Recommendation
  • Non-goals
  • Decision (added later)

items.prompt: What is the purpose of a 'Non-goals' section in an RFC?
choices: To explicitly state what the proposal is not trying to solve, so reviewers don't mistake scope creep or a missing feature for an oversight
To list out every possible future feature the team might conceivably decide to build someday
To preemptively apologize, in writing, for anything the finished RFC might happen to get wrong
It's essentially optional decoration in the template, with no real functional purpose behind it
items.explanation: Non-goals draws an explicit boundary around scope — without it, a reviewer might raise 'but what about X' as a blocking objection when X was never meant to be covered by this proposal at all, wasting a review cycle on a scope mismatch instead of a real trade-off.
items.reference:
• Context / problem
  • Options considered
  • Trade-offs (every option, including the pick)
  • Recommendation
  • Non-goals
  • Decision (added later)

items.prompt: What separates a blocking objection from a non-blocking comment?
choices: A blocking objection names a specific, checkable failure and typically a concrete alternative; a non-blocking comment (a preference or a vague question) doesn't gate anything
A blocking objection is, per this unit's stated rule, simply defined as any comment that happens to be left by someone senior on the team
A blocking objection is defined here as any comment that the author of the RFC personally happens to disagree with at the time
There's no meaningful difference described anywhere in this unit — every single comment should be treated as equally blocking regardless of content
items.explanation: The distinguishing feature is concreteness, not seniority or tone — a comment that names a specific failure mode the author can investigate is blocking regardless of who wrote it; a style preference or unspecific doubt isn't, no matter how senior the commenter.
items.reference:
Blocking

Specific, checkable failure + alternative

Non-blocking

Preference, vague doubt, no gate

items.prompt: A comment reads: 'I'm not sure this is the right call.' Is this blocking?
choices: No — it names no specific failure mode, so the author has nothing concrete to investigate or respond to
Yes, because per this unit's model any expression of doubt at all should halt the entire review process
Yes, but strictly only if that particular comment happens to come from the team's tech lead
It depends entirely on how many other people go on to 'like' or react positively to that same comment
items.explanation: Without a concrete, checkable claim attached, 'I'm not sure' is a feeling rather than a finding — there's nothing for the author to verify or argue against. Compare it to Marco's actual objection in L3, which named a specific timeout mismatch with a source.
items.reference:
Blocking

Specific, checkable failure + alternative

Non-blocking

Preference, vague doubt, no gate

items.prompt: A junior engineer's comment includes a specific calculation showing a proposal would double a cloud bill, with a source. A senior engineer's comment just says 'I don't love this.' Which one gates the decision, and on what basis?
choices: The junior engineer's comment — because it's concrete and checkable, not because of who wrote it
The senior engineer's, because seniority always outranks a junior's comment
Neither gates anything until a manager weighs in
Both gate equally, since both express disagreement
items.explanation: Blocking status comes from the content of the objection, not the rank of the person raising it. A worked-out, checkable claim gates the decision; an unspecific feeling doesn't, regardless of title — this is exactly what keeps review quality from becoming a function of hierarchy.
items.reference:
Blocking

Specific, checkable failure + alternative

Non-blocking

Preference, vague doubt, no gate

items.prompt: Why does an RFC need a named decision owner before review even opens?
choices: Without one, 'decision' quietly becomes 'whoever argues longest,' reproducing the live-thread failure mode inside a document
The owner role, in this process, is only really needed to format the document correctly before posting
Having a named decision owner is, per this unit, treated as a formal legal requirement at most companies
It genuinely doesn't matter who makes the call, as long as everyone eventually comes around to agreeing
items.explanation: Without an explicit decision-maker, disagreements have no tiebreaker — the loudest or most persistent voice ends up deciding by default, which is the same failure a live thread has, just dressed up in a written document.
items.reference:
Named owner breaks ties by design.
No owner = whoever argues longest wins, by accident.

items.prompt: Does disagree-and-commit mean the person who lost the argument has to pretend they now agree with the decision?
choices: No — it means stating the objection once on the record, then executing the decision at full effort without relitigating it
Yes, publicly claiming agreement is the whole point of the rule
Yes, and they should also stop mentioning the topic ever again, even with new evidence
No — it means they can keep arguing indefinitely as long as they still build the feature
items.explanation: Commit isn't about changing your stated opinion — the objection stays on the record. It's about behavior after the decision: full-effort execution instead of a slow-walked implementation or repeated relitigating without new evidence.
items.reference:
Named owner breaks ties by design.
No owner = whoever argues longest wins, by accident.

items.prompt: Marco's blocking objection delayed RFC-014's acceptance by one day. The RFC was still accepted, close to Priya's original proposal, just amended. Was the day of delay worth it?
choices: Yes — the objection caught a real bug (double-processed jobs) before implementation, which is far cheaper than catching it in production
No — since the final decision stayed close to the original, the objection didn't really change much and arguably wasted a day
Only in the specific case where it turns out that Marco happened to outrank Priya on the team
No — per this reasoning, objections should only ever be raised if they're guaranteed to change the final outcome
items.explanation: The objection's value isn't measured by how much it changed the final document — it's measured by where the bug got caught. A day of review delay is far cheaper than the same duplicate-processing bug surfacing after ship, discovered by customers instead of a reviewer.
items.reference:
Caught in review: 1 day delay, fixed calmly.
Caught in production: incident, rollback, customer impact.

items.prompt: In RFC-014, what made Marco's SQS visibility-timeout comment a blocking objection rather than noise?
choices: It named a specific, checkable failure (30s default timeout vs. 90s job runtime) with a source, and identified a concrete consequence (duplicate processing)
It was posted by one of the assigned reviewers, which per this process automatically makes any comment blocking
It happened to use the literal word 'blocking' somewhere in the text of the comment itself
It was simply the very first comment posted right after the review window had opened
items.explanation: What made it blocking was the content: a specific default value, a specific job runtime, a cited source, and a named consequence (double-processing) — exactly the kind of concrete, checkable claim L2 defined as gating, not the label or the timing of the comment.
items.reference:
Caught in review: 1 day delay, fixed calmly.
Caught in production: incident, rollback, customer impact.

items.prompt: If Marco had stayed silent about the visibility-timeout mismatch instead of raising it, what would most likely have happened, based on the worked example?
choices: The gap would probably have surfaced later in production, as silently duplicated image jobs, discovered after the fact instead of before ship
SQS itself would most likely have automatically detected and silently fixed the mismatch on its own
The RFC would most likely have been rejected outright, with no real path left to acceptance
Nothing would have been different — the same amendment would have happened anyway, with nobody needing to raise it
items.explanation: The mismatch (30s timeout vs. 90s job runtime) was a real, unaddressed gap in the original document — nothing in the RFC would have caught it automatically. Silence from Marco most plausibly means the gap ships as written and gets discovered by its actual symptom: jobs quietly processed twice.
items.reference:
Caught in review: 1 day delay, fixed calmly.
Caught in production: incident, rollback, customer impact.

items.prompt: Priya's trade-off table in RFC-014 lists a cost, risk, and 'what we give up' for Option A (SQS) — her own recommendation — as well as for Options B and C. Why does this matter?
choices: It lets a reviewer like Marco form an independent judgment instead of just reacting to Priya's conclusion, and it's part of what let him spot the timeout gap
It genuinely doesn't matter much — the recommended option's trade-offs are usually skipped in practice anyway
It's only ever strictly required for RFCs that happen to involve cloud infrastructure decisions specifically
It exists mainly, per this reasoning, just to pad out the overall length of the finished document
items.explanation: Rating the recommended option by the same honest standard as the rejected ones is what keeps a trade-off table from being a sales pitch. It's also structurally what gave Marco something concrete (Option A's row) to scrutinize and find the gap in.
items.reference: Rate every option — including the one you're recommending — by the same standard, or the table isn't a comparison, it's a pitch.

items.prompt: Suppose Priya had left Option A's trade-off row blank, listing costs only for Options B and C. What's the most likely consequence for the review process?
choices: Reviewers would have less material to scrutinize the recommended option, making a real gap like the timeout mismatch harder to catch
Nothing would really change here, since reviewers in practice tend to focus only on the recommendation section anyway
The RFC would, under this team's policy, automatically be rejected outright on procedural grounds
It would simply make the overall document easier and faster to read, with no real meaningful downside
items.explanation: An unscrutinized 'winning' option isn't actually reviewed, it's just announced. Marco's objection came from engaging with Option A's specifics; a blank row there removes exactly the surface a reviewer needs to find a real problem before it ships.
items.reference: Rate every option — including the one you're recommending — by the same standard, or the table isn't a comparison, it's a pitch.

items.prompt: A reviewer has real doubts about an RFC but says nothing during review, then criticizes the decision after it ships. What anti-pattern is this, and why is it worse than raising a loud objection?
choices: Silent disagreement — worse because the objection never existed on the record, so nobody could weigh or address it before the decision was made
Approval theater — worse because, in this case, a 👍 was given by someone without actually reading the document
Relitigating — worse because, in this scenario, the exact same argument ends up getting repeated again later
This isn't actually a real problem at all here, since the criticism did stem from a genuine, honestly-held concern
items.explanation: Silent disagreement denies the process the one thing it needs to work: the objection actually being visible before the decision is made. Criticizing afterward doesn't recover that — the concern arrives too late to be weighed against the decision, which makes it strictly worse than raising it loudly during review.
items.reference:
Silent disagreementDoubts never voiced, criticized later
RelitigatingSame rejected point, no new evidence
Vague objectionNo specific failure named
Approval theaterStamp with no real scrutiny
No named ownerDecision by loudest voice

items.prompt: Six weeks after RFC-014 was accepted, a teammate brings up the same rejected Redis-durability-layer argument again in an unrelated planning meeting, with no new information. What anti-pattern is this?
choices: Relitigating after commit — disagree-and-commit specifically requires new evidence to reopen a decision, not a restatement of the original argument
Silent disagreement, since in this specific case the objection was apparently never raised before this moment
Approval theater, since the original RFC-014 document had already been formally approved earlier
This is simply healthy, ongoing technical debate, and per this reasoning not really a problem at all
items.explanation: Bringing back a rejected argument with nothing new isn't renewed diligence, it's exactly what disagree-and-commit is designed to prevent — every decision would stay permanently provisional if any objection could be replayed indefinitely without new evidence.
items.reference:
Silent disagreementDoubts never voiced, criticized later
RelitigatingSame rejected point, no new evidence
Vague objectionNo specific failure named
Approval theaterStamp with no real scrutiny
No named ownerDecision by loudest voice

items.prompt: A reviewer leaves a 👍 on an RFC within thirty seconds of it being posted, without reading the trade-off table. What anti-pattern is this, and what does it defeat?
choices: Approval theater — it defeats the point of async review, since the document gets a stamp without getting the scrutiny that could catch a real gap
Relitigating — in this case it defeats the underlying point of disagree-and-commit as a practice
Vague objection — here it defeats the specific point of naming an explicit, accountable decision owner
This is actually fine and, per this unit's model, exactly how asynchronous review is supposed to work
items.explanation: A quick approval with no real reading is a stamp, not review — it looks like scrutiny happened when it didn't. This is precisely the gap that let a Marco-style objection slip through in a team culture where 👍-without-reading is normal.
items.reference:
Silent disagreementDoubts never voiced, criticized later
RelitigatingSame rejected point, no new evidence
Vague objectionNo specific failure named
Approval theaterStamp with no real scrutiny
No named ownerDecision by loudest voice

items.prompt: Suppose Priya had disagreed with Marco's timeout math instead of confirming it. Could she still have proceeded with the original proposal?
choices: Yes, but disagree-and-commit would require her to write the reasoning for overruling into the document, not just proceed silently
No — under this process, a named decision owner can never overrule a genuinely blocking objection
Yes, and no further explanation would be required of her at all since she's the designated decision owner
No — in that case the entire RFC would instead have to be withdrawn and abandoned altogether
items.explanation: An owner can overrule a blocking objection, but the process still requires the reasoning to be on the record — 'acknowledged, and overruled, for this specific reason' — rather than simply outvoting the objection by staying silent on it.
items.reference: Overrule is allowed — but the reasoning must be written into the record, same as an amendment would be.

items.prompt: Why does an overruled objection still need a written reason, even though the owner is allowed to proceed anyway?
choices: So the decision is demonstrably made with the objection accounted for, not just ignored — the same transparency an amendment would have gotten
It genuinely doesn't need one at all — the owner's formal authority alone is treated as a sufficient reason on its own
It exists only to satisfy some external, unrelated compliance requirement imposed on the team from outside
So that the objecting reviewer can later be formally and officially overruled in a separate follow-up document
items.explanation: Writing the reasoning down is what distinguishes 'the objection was heard and weighed' from 'the objection was ignored.' Without it, an overrule looks identical to authority simply winning by default — the exact failure mode a named-owner process is supposed to avoid.
items.reference: Overrule is allowed — but the reasoning must be written into the record, same as an amendment would be.

items.prompt: An RFC's decision log reads only 'Accepted — 2026-02-13,' with no mention of the blocking objection that was raised during review. What's the problem with this record?
choices: It erases whether the objection was addressed, amended for, or overruled — someone reading it later can't tell if the concern was actually resolved
There's genuinely no real problem here; per this model a decision log only ever needs a date and a status field
It's only actually a problem in cases where the objection later turns out to have been technically correct
It's fine as it stands, since the original objection is still technically visible somewhere in the comment thread
items.explanation: A decision log that omits how a real objection was handled loses exactly the information that makes disagree-and-commit trustworthy — future readers (or the objector themselves) can't verify whether the concern was actually accounted for versus quietly dropped.
items.reference: Overrule is allowed — but the reasoning must be written into the record, same as an amendment would be.

items.prompt: Two reviewers raise blocking objections that genuinely conflict — satisfying one design requirement would violate the other. Who resolves this, according to the process described?
choices: A named decision-maker above both reviewers, via the escalation path, rather than the author picking a side alone
Whichever of the two reviewers happens to have more seniority automatically wins the disagreement outright
The two conflicting objections simply cancel each other out, so neither one actually needs to be addressed
Per this process, the entire RFC must be abandoned altogether with no resolution reached at all
items.explanation: A conflict between two well-evidenced objections isn't something the author can resolve alone without effectively picking a side unilaterally — this is exactly the case that needs L2's escalation path: a named decision-maker positioned above both reviewers.
items.reference: Same author. Same reviewer. Different concern each time — RFC-014's mechanics generalize; the escalation path is what handles cases this specific example didn't need.

items.prompt: A security reviewer outside the immediate team raises a blocking objection on an RFC, and the author disagrees that it matters. How does this differ from Marco's objection in RFC-014, in terms of what's needed to resolve it?
choices: It more plausibly needs the L2 escalation path (a decision-maker above both parties), since it crosses team boundaries rather than being resolved within the author's own investigation
It genuinely doesn't differ in any meaningful way — per this reasoning the author should just decide unilaterally either way, regardless of who raised it
Cross-team objections are, under this unit's process, automatically and categorically treated as non-blocking by default, no matter their content
It requires no resolution at all in this case, simply because the reviewer in question wasn't part of the original project team to begin with
items.explanation: Marco's objection was resolved by the author investigating and amending within her own authority. A cross-team disagreement where the author disputes the objection's relevance is a different shape of problem — it's exactly the kind of case L2 flagged as needing a decision-maker positioned above both sides, not the author unilaterally overruling an outside reviewer.
items.reference: Same author. Same reviewer. Different concern each time — RFC-014's mechanics generalize; the escalation path is what handles cases this specific example didn't need.

items.prompt: Why does the L3 unit explicitly say the RFC-014 worked example is 'one instance of the process, not the whole shape of what it has to handle'?
choices: Because RFC-014 involved a single, cooperative objection resolved by the author alone — other real cases (conflicting objections, cross-team disputes) need mechanisms the example didn't exercise, like escalation
Because RFC-014, as presented throughout this unit's narrative, wasn't actually a real example at all and therefore shouldn't be trusted as representative
Because, per this unit's own explicit claim, literally every single RFC follows an identical script regardless of who happens to be involved
Because the lifecycle stages that were carefully described back in L2 are said here to simply not apply to real-world RFCs at all
items.explanation: RFC-014 is a clean, single-objection case that the author resolved through her own investigation — useful for seeing the mechanics concretely, but not a stand-in for every case. Conflicting objections or a disputed cross-team concern need the escalation path from L2, which this particular example never had to invoke.
items.reference: Same author. Same reviewer. Different concern each time — RFC-014's mechanics generalize; the escalation path is what handles cases this specific example didn't need.
